{{Infobox Election | election_name = United States House of Representatives elections in Maine, 2018 | country = Maine | type = legislative | ongoing = yes | previous_election = United States House of Representatives elections in Maine, 2016 | previous_year = 2016 | next_election = United States House of Representatives elections in Maine, 2020 | next_year = 2020 | seats_for_election = Both Maine seats to the [[United States House of Representatives]] | election_date = {{Start date|2018|11|06}} | party1 = Democratic Party (United States) | last_election1 = 1 | seats1 = | seat_change1 = | popular_vote1 = | percentage1 = | swing1 = | party2 = Republican Party (United States) | last_election2 = 1 | seats2 = | seat_change2 = | popular_vote2 = | percentage2 = | swing2 = | map_image = | map_caption = }} {{ElectionsME}} The '''2018 United States House of Representatives elections in Maine''' will be held on November 6, 2018, to elect the two [[United States House of Representatives|U.S. Representatives]] from the [[U.S. state|state]] of [[Maine]], one from each of the state's two [[Maine's congressional districts|congressional districts]]. The elections will coincide with [[United States Senate election in Maine, 2018|elections]] to the [[United States Senate]], [[Maine gubernatorial election, 2018|a gubernatorial election]], and various [[United States elections, 2018#State elections|state]] and [[United States elections, 2018#Local elections|local elections]]. These U.S. House elections will be conducted with [[Instant-runoff voting|ranked choice voting]], as opposed to a simple plurality, after Maine voters passed [[Maine Question 5, 2016|a citizen referendum]] approving the change in 2016{{cite news|title=Maine became the first state in the country Tuesday to pass ranked choice voting|url=https://www.boston.com/news/politics/2016/11/10/maine-became-the-first-state-in-the-country-to-pass-ranked-choice-voting|accessdate=17 November 2016|newspaper=Boston Globe|date=10 November 2016}}and a June 2018 referendum sustaining the change.{{cite news|title=Maine Voters Overrule Their Leaders|url=https://www.theatlantic.com/politics/archive/2018/06/maine-lepage-ranked-choice-voting/562871/|accessdate=24 June 2018|newspaper=The Atlantic|date= 15 June 2018}} Ranked choice voting was used in the primary elections as well.{{cite web|url=https://www.miamiherald.com/news/politics-government/national-politics/article213587154.html|title=Ranked-choice voting fans hope Maine's experiment pays off|date=21 June 2018}} {{Toclimit|limit=2}} ==District 1== {{see also|Maine's 1st congressional district}} [[Chellie Pingree]], the [[incumbent]] representative, was first elected in [[United States House of Representatives elections in Maine, 2008|2008]], and in [[United States House of Representatives elections in Maine, 2016|2016]] defeated Republican nominee Mark Holbrook with just under 58 percent of the vote. Holbrook ran again for the Republican nomination, and was unopposed. Independent State Representative Marty Grohman, elected as a Democrat in the 2016 State House election, defected the party in 2017. He launched his campaign for the first district in spring 2018. Due to the use of [[ranked choice voting]] in the election, Pingree may be vulnerable if she does not win outright in the first round, as Grohman could be a second choice for Republican and Democratic voters. {{cite web|url=https://www.pressherald.com/2018/05/29/grohman-makes-the-ballot-as-an-independent-in-race-for-maines-1st-congressional-district/|title=State lawmaker submits enough signatures to challenge Rep. Pingree|work=[[Portland Press Herald]]|author=Scott Thistle|date=May 29, 2018 |accessdate=August 30, 2018}} Grohman is receiving substantial support from Republican elected officials and activists, including Republican Governor [[Paul LePage]] and the State Director of President [[Donald Trump]]'s [[Donald Trump presidential campaign, 2016|2016 presidential campaign]] Christie-Lee McNally. Poliquin ran for the Republican nomination unopposed. Cain did not challenge Poliquin again, instead taking a job with the progressive group [[EMILY's List|Emily's List]]. Initially, six candidates filed for the Democratic nomination — [[United States Postal Service]] employee and activist Phil Cleaves, carpenter and former Maine State Senate candidate Jonathan Fulford, Assistant Majority Leader of the State House of Representatives [[Jared Golden]], shopkeeper and former Chair of the [[Islesboro, Maine|Isleboro]] Board of Selectmen Craig Olson, businessman and former State Senate candidate Tim Rich, and conservationist Lucas St. Clair. Cleaves, Rich and Fulford dropped out at various points in the campaign, though Fulford's withdrawal happened too late for his name to be removed from the primary ballot. Several candidates received prominent endorsements; St. Clair was endorsed by the [[League of Conservation Voters]] and California Congressman [[Jared Huffman]], Fulford by the left-wing group [[Our Revolution]] prior to his withdrawal from the race, and Golden by [[VoteVets.org|VoteVets]], Massachusetts Congressman [[Seth Moulton]] and over two dozen members of the Maine Legislature. Golden defeated St. Clair and Olson on the second ballot after [[Instant-runoff voting|ranked choice voting]]. In addition, two third-party candidates announced their candidacies for the seat: [[Houlton Band of Maliseet Indians|Houlton Band of Maliseets]] State Representative [[Henry John Bear]] of the [[Maine Green Independent Party]] and Brian Kresge of the [[Libertarian Party of Maine|Libertarian Party]]. Bear, a former Democrat, left the party due to its stance on water rights for Maine's native people. He failed to qualify for the ballot. Kresge, a veteran and writer, withdrew from the race to run for a seat in the State House of Representatives. Neither the Libertarians nor Green Independents will have a candidate on the ballot. Two independent candidates qualified for the ballot: Tiffany Bond, an attorney from [[Portland, Maine|Portland]] (a city outside of the second district), and Will Hoar, a schoolteacher. ===Democratic
